crossref.title: Opening Letter of RILEM TC-MCA: Mechano-chemical activation of cementitious constituents
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Mechano-chemical activation has drawn increasing attention in recent years for its capacity to increase the reactivity of cementitious constituents and valorise waste streams. We define mechano-chemical activation as a change in the structure and/or chemistry of a material which accelerates its dissolution and participation in subsequent formation of reaction products, that is caused via mechanical energy supplied through a mechanical treatment. The potential advantages of mechano-chemical activation have driven growing numbers of promising laboratory-scale studies on numerous materials. Yet numerous knowledge gaps still need to be resolved. We highlight five key knowledge gaps in this topic: the a priori susceptibility of different material categories to mechano-chemical activation; influence of processing parameters across mill types; structural/property indicators; performance indicators; and, processing-property-performance relationships. The approach of TC-MCA is to carry out interlaboratory testing experiments to resolve specific outstanding questions within these knowledge gaps, that cannot be addressed by a single laboratory. Improved understanding of mechano-chemical activation at the laboratory scale is a necessary preliminary step to assess its likely value at industrial scale. </jats:p>

Mechanical Properties and Durability Analysis of Hematite Concrete After High-Temperature Exposure
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>In this study, hematite was adopted as both coarse and fine aggregates to prepare hematite concrete with three strength grades of C40, C50 and C60. Specimens of hematite concrete subjected to five temperature levels were tested for mass loss ratio, compressive strength and flexural strength. Durability tests including chloride penetration test and sulfate attack test were also carried out. The results show that the mass loss ratio of hematite concrete increases continuously with the rise in exposure temperature. At 600 °C, the residual compressive strength ratios of C40, C50 and C60 specimens are 55.15%, 61.85% and 64.02%, respectively. At 450 °C, the flexural strength of specimens of all three strength grades retains only approximately 50% of the room-temperature value. This indicates that flexural performance is more sensitive to thermal damage than compressive performance. After high-temperature exposure, the chloride diffusion coefficient increases exponentially with temperature. At 600 °C, the diffusion coefficients of C40, C50 and C60 specimens are about 30 times those at room temperature. The pore sizes of specimens under ambient temperature are mainly distributed in the range of 10–100 nm. After high-temperature exposure, the proportion of small pores decreases, while the proportion of harmful pores with pore size larger than 1000 nm increases. At 600 °C, the pore size distribution shifts toward the range of 1000–10,000 nm. Within the temperature range of 25–300 °C, the corrosion resistance coefficients of all specimens remain above 95%, demonstrating excellent sulfate attack resistance in this temperature interval. At 450 °C, the corrosion resistance coefficient decreases continuously with the extension of erosion age. At 600 °C, the corrosion resistance coefficient of C40 specimens drops to 73.2%, below the durability threshold.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Study of Gas Release Kinetics in Mortar Mixtures and the Properties of Non-Autoclaved Aerated Concrete
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The object of this study is the process of gas release and pore formation in mortar mixtures during the production of non-autoclaved aerated concrete. The study addresses the problem of determining optimal technological parameters for regulating gas release kinetics in order to obtain aerated concrete with reduced density and sufficient compressive strength. The aim of the research was to investigate the kinetics of gas release in mortar mixtures and to determine the influence of calcined soda, caustic soda, and mixture temperature on the formation processes and physical-mechanical properties of non-autoclaved aerated concrete. The experimental methodology included laboratory studies using mathematical planning of experiments and statistical data processing in the STATISTICA 12 software environment. A specially designed experimental device equipped with an electronic data acquisition module was used to monitor the swelling process and determine the onset, duration, and intensity of gas release. The obtained results demonstrated that both the temperature of the mortar mixture and the dosage of additives significantly affect gas release kinetics and pore structure formation. Optimal technological parameters were established at an additive content of 0.6 % and a mixture temperature of 40–41 °C. Under these conditions, accelerated swelling of the mixture was achieved, while the average density of aerated concrete samples decreased to 820 kg/m³ and compressive strength reached 3.8 MPa. The use of the investigated additives made it possible to eliminate the preliminary heating stage of the mixture, thereby reducing energy consumption and simplifying the manufacturing process. The study established the relationship between gas release kinetics and the physical-mechanical properties of non-autoclaved aerated concrete. The proposed methodology and developed experimental device enable optimization of mixture composition and technological parameters, ensuring stable quality of aerated concrete under both laboratory and industrial production conditions.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Comparative Analysis between Conventional Concrete and UHPC with GGBFS in PCI Girder Bridge Construction
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Precast Concrete I-Girder (PCI girder) bridges are typically utilized for short to medium spans due to their ease of construction. However, the demand for longer spans and sustainability in bridge construction has prompted the use of higher-performance and lower-carbon-emitting materials in constructions. Materials like Ultra-High Performance Concrete (UHPC) offer high levels of strength and durability to the bridges, while Ground Granulated Blast Furnace Slag (GGBFS) reduces the amount of cement. This study investigates the use of UHPC with GGBFS in PCI girder bridges. A comparison between a conventional concrete two-span bridge and a UHPC with GGBFS single-span bridge is conducted, including their structure, the amount of material required for construction, construction costs, carbon emissions, and construction duration. The structural analysis of the bridges was performed using Midas Civil 2025. Material take-off and cost estimation was performed using Indonesian Unit Price Analysis (called Analisis Harga Satuan Pekerjaan or AHSP). The environmental impact was assessed through cradle-to-gate Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) analysis. The results indicate that the use of UHPC with GGBFS allows for a single-span bridge of the same dimensions as the two-span concrete bridge, whereby it requires less reinforcement and reduces carbon emissions of 9.77% due to the elimination of the middle pier. While construction costs for the UHPC with GGBFS bridge are higher, construction time is shortened from 51 to 38 weeks due to the elimination of the bridge pier. Overall, the use of UHPC with GGBFS provides structural, sustainability, and construction time benefits but at a higher cost.</jats:p>

A novel carbon dioxide-cured cement coating for steel slag aggregates to enhance concrete performance
crossref.container: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Structures and Buildings
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The use of steel slag aggregates in concrete supports waste valorisation and sustainable construction, but their poor volumetric stability causes expansion-induced cracking and concrete deterioration. A novel carbonated cement coating was developed through three cycles of cement packaging and carbonation curing. Carbonated cement-coated slag (CCS) was evaluated against water-cured hydrated cement-coated slag (HCS). Mercury intrusion porosimetry and X-ray diffraction characterised the coating’s pore structure and phases; aggregate properties, concrete strength and long-term stability were evaluated. Carbonation reduced coating porosity from 20% to 16% and converted portlandite to calcite and vaterite, forming a denser, more robust coating. Relative to HCS, CCS reduced water absorption from 3.63% to 2.75%, crushing value from 5.14% to 4.07% and autoclave pulverisation rate from 1.82% to 1.07%. CCS concrete reached 41.3 MPa and 51.5 MPa at 7 days and 28 days, respectively. During elevated-temperature curing, it maintained an intact surface and gained strength to 58.8 MPa at 90 days, whereas concrete containing untreated steel slag lost strength and deteriorated. These results demonstrate that carbonation rapidly creates a dense, robust coating that suppresses steel slag expansion, improves aggregate and concrete performance and supports large-scale steel slag utilisation in durable, sustainable concrete.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Enhancement of gamma radiation shielding performance of heavyweight concrete using slag and Direct Reduced Iron (DRI)
crossref.container: Journal of Umm Al-Qura University for Engineering and Architecture
crossref.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The effectiveness of shielding concrete in nuclear and medical facilities depends primarily on its density and radiation attenuation capacity. This study investigates the use of steel slag and direct reduced iron (DRI), two locally available industrial by-products, as heavyweight aggregates for enhancing gamma radiation shielding performance of concrete. An experimental program was conducted on concrete cube specimens and prismatic beams prepared with full replacement of conventional dolomite coarse aggregate and natural sand by slag-, iron powder-, and DRI-based aggregates. The main study variables were aggregate type and water-to-cement (w/c) ratio (0.40 and 0.50) resulting in a total of twelve mixtures. A conventional concrete mix containing dolomite and sand was used as the control specimen for comparison. The investigation included physical characterization (specific gravity and water absorption), mechanical testing (compressive and flexural strength), UPV measurements before and after irradiation, and gamma attenuation assessment through determination of the linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) and half-value layer (HVL). Concrete specimens with varying thicknesses were exposed to a Cesium-137 (Cs-137) gamma source emitting photons at 662 keV under narrow-beam transmission geometry. Results showed that heavyweight mixes incorporating slag and DRI achieved significantly higher LAC values and lower HVL compared to the control concrete. The best-performing mix exhibited an HVL of 2.09 cm, approximately 48% lower than the control mix, demonstrating superior shielding efficiency. This improvement was primarily attributed to the use of high-density slag and iron-based aggregates, which constituted the most influential variable governing radiation attenuation performance. Slag-based mixes also maintained or improved mechanical strength, while short-term irradiation (7 days) caused no significant internal integrity changes. These findings confirm that steel industry by-products can serve as sustainable and cost-effective alternatives to conventional heavyweight aggregates for structural gamma radiation shielding applications.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the inter-test correlation between various early-age characteristics of complex cementitious systems. The correlations are used for predicting physical and chemical processes in portland cement–based systems with different chemical and physical accelerators. Correlations were established between the heat of hydration (HoH), ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV), setting time, compressive strength, and hydrate phases for cement pastes and mortars. When controlling for accelerator type/dosage, temperature, or water-to-cement ratio, correlating HoH to UPV for cement pastes demonstrated R2 values &gt;0.90, indicating reliability when controlled. However, when testing on mortar samples, a reduction in R2 to 0.75 was observed, marking the principal limitation of correlating these two tests. Predicting compressive strength based on HoH when controlling for the water-to-cement ratio or temperature resulted in correlations of R2 = 0.81 and R2 = 0.86, respectively. The main limitation was again when switching to mortar samples, which demonstrated an R2 of 0.66 at sand-to-cement ratio (S/C) = 1.5.</jats:p>

Early Hydration and Drying Shrinkage of Manufactured Sand Mortar: Effects of Limestone and Granite Powder
crossref.container: Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study systematically investigates the effects of limestone powder (LP) and granite powder (GP) on the early hydration and drying shrinkage behavior of manufactured sand (MS) mortar. The early hydration process of the cementitious system was monitored in real time using ultrasonic testing technology. Mechanisms of action were further elucidated through the Krstulović–Dabić hydration kinetic model, X-ray diffraction (XRD), chemical bound water analysis, and drying shrinkage tests. Results show that LP accelerates early hydration by providing nucleation sites and promoting the formation of hydration products, thereby leading to a denser microstructure. In contrast, GP acts mainly through dilution and physical barrier effects, which delay hydration and reduce the overall volume of hydration products. Both types of stone powder effectively mitigate early drying shrinkage of MS mortar, with GP showing superior shrinkage reduction (9%–28%) compared with LP (5%–20%) at equal replacement levels. This research provides theoretical support for the sustainable utilization of stone powder in MS mortar and for controlling its volume stability.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Sustainable Design of Lightweight Low-Clinker Mortars Incorporating Recycled Ceramic Constituents
crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of lightweight low-clinker cementitious materials requires simultaneous optimization of mechanical performance, density, workability, and sustainability.This study investigates the combined effects of ceramic brick powder, sodium sulphate, and cellulose ether on lightweight slag-cement mortars incorporating recycled ceramic fine aggregate. A D-optimal experimental design coupled with response surface methodology was employed to develop predictive experimental-statistical models. Fresh-state performance was evaluated through the superplasticizer demand required to maintain a constant flow spread of 140-150 mm, while hardened properties included density, compressive strength, flexural strength, and structural efficiency. The developed models were validated experimentally, yielding prediction errors below 3%. The investigated mortars achieved 28-day dry densities of 1790-1850 kg/m³, compressive strengths of 52-58 MPa, and flexural strengths of 7.6-8.8 MPa.Response surface analysis demonstrated that the engineering performance was governed by the combined interaction of varied composition factors. A constraint-based optimization identified an optimum mixture incorporating approximately 249 kg/m³ of ceramic brick powder while satisfying the target requirements for compressive strength (≥55 MPa), flexural strength (≥8 MPa), and dry density (≤1820 kg/m³). Compared with the reference mixture, the optimized composition reduced cement consumption by approximately 32%, corresponding to estimated reductions of about 119 kg CO₂-eq./m³ and 0.69 GJ/m³ of embodied energy. The proposed methodology provides an effective framework for designing resource-efficient lightweight structural mortars containing recycled ceramic constituents.</jats:p>

crossref.title: Mechanical Performance of Shotcrete Concrete Using Different Local Sourced Aggregates in Nepal
crossref.container: Journal of Engineering Technology and Planning
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Wet-mix shotcrete is extensively used in tunnel lining, slope stabilization, and rock bolting in Nepal, as there has been an increase in the need for this sprayed concrete with respect to infrastructure construction in difficult to reach Himalayan areas of Nepal. Aggregate quality and its source significantly affect the effectiveness of shotcrete application, however, the mixture of shotcrete in Nepal is often developed according to specifications that are used abroad. The rivers Seti and Kali Gandaki are one of the main sources of aggregates in Nepal, but no comparative study on the influence of both rivers on shotcrete’s physical properties has ever been done. The current research is focused on analyzing C30 class wet-mix shotcrete manufactured using OPC 53 class cement and aggregates of two sources: Seti River (A) and Kali Gandaki River (B). In total, six mixes were prepared using polycarboxylate-based superplasticizer PC 30H with water to cement ratio of 0.30, 0.35 and 0.40 for both sources. Workability was checked by slump test method and strength properties were determined after 1, 3, 7 and 28 days. All mixes met the C30 criterion. Mixes made with source A exhibited considerably higher compressive and flexural strength than those made with source B, indicating that source of aggregates is a determining variable in shotcrete performance. The maximum 28-day compressive strength of 45.17 MPa was recorded for mix M1A (Source A, w/c = 0.30). Compressive strength declined with increasing water cement ratio. These results represent the first data on the performance of shotcrete using aggregates from these sources in Nepal. The two sources will be able to satisfy C30 criteria, while source A along with lower water cement ratio (0.30 to 0.35) would be preferred where high early strength and 28 days strength is required such as tunnel support and slope stabilization. The limitations of the study involve the use of just two sources of aggregates, one type of cement and admixture and testing through laboratory-made specimens.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The growing demand for durable and sustainable construction materials has intensified research on alkali-activated binders as low-carbon alternatives to portland cement. One-part geopolymers offer practical advantages for field application; however, their long-term durability is strongly influenced by admixture compatibility, particularly superplasticizers, which can alter pore structure and chemical stability. This study investigates the influence of sulfonated naphthalene formaldehyde (SNF) and polycarboxylate ether (PCE) superplasticizers on the durability of a ternary one-part geopolymer system formulated from ground granulated blast-furnace slag, diatomite, and feldspar. Three mortar mixes were prepared: M1-N (1% SNF), M2-P (1% PCE), and M3-C (control without superplasticizer). Durability performance was assessed through acid resistance, sulfate resistance, water absorption, rapid chloride permeability test (RCPT), rapid chloride migration test (RCMT), and oxygen permeability. Microstructural analyses were conducted through X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Under sulfuric acid exposure, the SNF-modified system showed the lowest mass loss after 180 days (1.39%) and the highest residual compressive strength, retaining about 48% of its unexposed 28-day strength, compared with 44% for the PCE-modified mix and 41% for the control. crossref.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Alkali-activated materials (AAMs) are widely used for the treatment of chloride-rich municipal solid waste incineration fly ash (MSWI FA). However, there is a lack of study on the influence of inevitable CO32- and SO42- from MSWI FA on the chloride binding capacity of AAMs. In this study, AAMs with different levels of internal Cl-, SO42- and CO32- were prepared to simulate the systems with MSWI FA to provide insights into the intricate competition of three anions for being bound by in-situ formed hydrotalcites (Ht) in AAMs. The results showed that at 5 wt% internal Cl-, CO32- reduced bound chloride by 0.81~3.4%, whereas SO42- increased it by 3.7~10.2%, and the influence of both anions decreased with prolonging curing time from 7d to 28d. Ht formation in AAMs with 3 wt% Cl- increased from 5.6 wt% to 6.3 wt% and to 7.1 wt% with the presence of CO32- and SO42-, respectively, while an increase in Cl- from 3 wt% to 5 wt% slightly varied the Ht content. Cold-water extraction for chloride binding capacity quantification varied the phase assemblage due to dissolution, and the optimal extraction time was 2h for powder samples. Spatial distribution of Ht was obtained by quantitative SEM-EDS hypermaps analysis, which revealed that Ca-Al Ht and Mg-Al Ht coexisted around GGBS, but Cl- and SO42- showed preference for intercalation into the Ca-Al Ht. The SO42- from dissolved GGBS competed with Cl- for intercalating into Ht, and the statistic distribution of S and Cl in the Ht formed in AAMs was probably independent of the relative concentration of two anions in the raw materials. The findings suggest that stabilizing the sulfate by other phases rather than Ht to reduce the competition with chloride is vital to achieve high chloride binding by Ht in AAMs with MSWI FA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>As a potential supplementary cementitious material (SCM) for concrete, tuff rock powder has attracted increasing attention owing to its hydration activity and its influence on concrete durability. In this study, the effects of tuff rock powder on the hydration process and sulfate corrosion resistance of cement-based materials were systematically investigated by means of XRF, XRD, SEM, and TG-DTA analyses, mechanical property tests, and dry–wet cycling tests in sulfate solutions. The results indicate that: (1) at a tuff rock powder content of 15%, the 28 d compressive strength ratio reached 77.5%, which is close to that of fly ash; (2) under sulfate dry–wet cycling, the mass loss rate, the compressive strength corrosion resistance coefficient, and the electrical resistivity of C30 and C50 concrete all first increased and then decreased with increasing rock powder content, following a quadratic parabolic trend; (3) the addition of tuff rock powder triggers coupled mass gain and structural damage in concrete under sulfate attack, and the mass-gain effect dominates within a certain range to achieve the peak post-exposure compressive strength, corresponding to optimal dosages of 3.5–4.5% for C30 and 5–6% for C50 concrete.</jats:p>

Research Progress on the Tensile Properties of Engineered Cementitious Composites
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Engineered cementitious composites (ECC) exhibit tensile strain hardening and multiple cracking, providing a means of overcoming the limited tensile deformation capacity of conventional concrete. This review summarizes recent studies on the tensile behavior of ECC, with particular attention to stress–strain responses and crack control mechanisms. It examines the effects of fiber type, content and orientation, matrix composition, fiber–matrix interfaces, and temperature. Applications in bridge deck link slabs, structural repair and strengthening, additive construction, and marine infrastructure are also discussed. The reviewed studies indicate that tensile performance depends on the coordinated design of fibers, matrix, and interfaces. Further research should address material cost, fiber dispersion, construction methods, and the optimization of mixtures incorporating industrial and agricultural by-products.</jats:p>

Mechanical Properties of Ultra-High-Performance Concrete Reinforced with Hybrid Fibers
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>We compared nine ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) mixtures, including a plain reference and eight mixtures containing 2.0 vol% short steel, long steel, or polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fibers in different proportions. The equal-volume steel blend M4 had a flexural strength of 27.0 MPa and a reported fracture energy of 31.5 kJ/m2, 25.3% and 52.5% above the corresponding volume-weighted single-steel baselines. M7 had the highest reported compressive strength and elastic modulus, at 151.6 MPa and 48.0 GPa. Replacing 0.25 vol% short steel with long steel from M7 to M8 was associated with a rise in flexural strength from 29.2 to 30.4 MPa and in reported fracture energy from 35.8 to 38.6 kJ/m2. The reported compressive strength was 1.2% lower. In M8, PVA occupied 12.5% of the fiber volume and accounted for 89.3% of the calculated filament count and 45.5% of the calculated lateral interface area. The mixture comparisons suggest that longer potential steel-fiber embedment may contribute to resistance during crack opening.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the effects of fiber type and cover thickness of ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) on rebar corrosion protection in accelerated corrosion testing. Three UHPCs with steel-fiber-reinforced (UF0.5, 0.5 vol%), glass-fiber-reinforced (UG0.5, 0.5 vol%), and stainless-steel wire mesh (UWMT2.5) were applied as 25 mm UHPC covers over reinforced concrete (RC) samples under accelerated corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for 150 days. UF0.5 covers at two thicknesses (20 mm, T2.0; 25 mm, T2.5) were additionally evaluated. Performance was assessed using the rebar mass loss ratio (Mloss), six-position chloride-ion profiles spanning both the UHPC cover and the underlying substrate, the connected porosity ratio, scanning electron microscopy, and mechanical properties. UHPC covering RC substantially outperformed the RC reference (Mloss = 100 %). UHPC with wire mesh (UWMT2.5) clearly reduced Mloss (80.61 %). Glass-fiber UHPC (UG0.5T2.5, Mloss = 33.91 %) further improved protection, while steel-fiber UHPC delivered the best corrosion protection: Mloss = 23.18 % (T2.5) and 23.80 % (T2.0). The Cl- content of the steel-fiber UHPC cover was lower than that of the RC substrate and other UHPC covers. A 20 mm steel-fiber UHPC cover may be a potential cover thickness to enhance corrosion protection of RC.</jats:p>

crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The deterioration caused by chloride ion is one of the main factors limiting the long-term durability of concrete structures in marine and coastal environments. In order to alleviate chloride ion migration related to shrinkage-induced defects and cracks at the same time, a combined modification strategy of MgO expansive agent (MEA) combined with steel fiber was proposed to improve the chloride ion resistance of concrete. Six concrete mixtures were tested in 3% NaCl solution at seven exposure ages. The chloride concentration distribution at different depths was measured, and the apparent diffusion coefficient was determined according to Fick’s second law. The results showed that with the increase in penetration depth, the concentration of chloride ion gradually decreased, and gradually stabilized at about 10–12 mm. Compared with ordinary concrete, an appropriate volume fraction of steel fiber (1.0%) and MEA dosage (8% by mass of cement and fly ash) can reduce the chloride ion diffusion coefficient of concrete by 12.9% and 13.3% at 30 days, respectively, while excessive volume fraction of steel fiber (1.5%) and MgO content (10%) will increase the chloride ion diffusion coefficient possibly owing to interfacial effects and expansion, respectively. A mixture of 8% MgO and 1.0% steel fiber had the best effect, and the chloride ion diffusion coefficient was reduced by 30.0%, indicating that the composite doping had a beneficial combined effect on chloride ion resistance. By introducing the attenuation law of apparent surface chloride concentration and diffusion coefficient, a time-dependent chloride diffusion model was established. Measured profiles at 50 and 100 days were withheld from fitting and used to evaluate the predicted concentration profiles. The combined mixture showed improved resistance to chloride ingress under the immersion conditions examined, providing experimental evidence for material selection in chloride-exposed structures.</jats:p>

Reinforcement Corrosion in Coral Aggregate Concrete: 20-Month In-Situ Comparison of Portland, Magnesium Phosphate, and Hybrid Fly Ash–Silica Fume Binders in the South China Sea
crossref.container: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Reinforcement corrosion is a governing durability concern for coral aggregate concrete (CAC) structures in the South China Sea, yet long-term field evidence comparing alternative binder systems under natural marine exposure remains scarce. This study reports a 20-month in-situ exposure campaign on a natural reef-flat platform in Zhanjiang Bay, in which HRB400 carbon steel and 316L stainless steel rebars were embedded in CAC prepared with Portland cement (PC), magnesium phosphate cement (MPC), and a hybrid fly ash–silica fume binder (HF) at a fixed water-to-binder ratio of 0.30. Open-circuit potential was monitored over early (0–5 months), middle (5–12 months), and late (12–20 months) exposure windows, and potentiodynamic polarization was measured at three snapshot ages (month 5; months 12–14; months 19–20), complemented by rapid chloride migration testing, XRD, and SEM–EDS. The corrosion behavior of carbon steel was strongly binder-dependent. In the MPC matrix, carbon steel underwent severe early-stage activation (icorr = 7.92 µA/cm2, equivalent to 91.9 µm/y), which is attributed to the near-neutral pore solution of the portlandite-free K-struvite matrix; the corrosion rate subsequently decreased by more than four orders of magnitude, a trend consistent with a transition toward transport-limited kinetics rather than a restoration of passivity. The HF binder yielded the lowest chloride migration coefficient (0.171 × 10−12 m2/s) and sustained low corrosion rates of carbon steel, plausibly reflecting pozzolanic pore refinement and chloride binding. 316L stainless steel remained below the RILEM TC 154-EMC passivity threshold (0.1 µA/cm2) in all three binders. These results suggest that binder–reinforcement compatibility, rather than matrix density alone, governs the long-term corrosion performance of CAC in reef-flat environments.</jats:p>

<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Objective.</jats:bold>
                    The development of the global cement industry and the chemistry of binders dictates the need for more in-depth research and development of a variety of clinker products using nano, ultra, and fine-grained additives of man-made or natural origin. Practical experience with composite cements using active and inert mineral, complex, and organomineral additives is quite extensive. It is the mechanical and mechanochemical activation of mineral additives that allows for the opening of active crystallization centers on the surface of a solid, increasing its free energy and reactivity.
                    <jats:bold>Method.</jats:bold>
                    The tests were carried out in accordance with GOST 310.4-81 Cements. Methods for Determining Bending and Compressive Strength; GOST 310.3-76 Cements. Methods for Determining Normal Density, Setting Time, and Uniformity of Volume Change.
                    <jats:bold>Result.</jats:bold>
                    Formulations have been developed and the properties of low-clinker binders have been studied using mechanochemically activated additives made from cullet and calcined argillite. Analysis of the obtained results for low-clinker binders revealed a significant increase in compressive and flexural strength. The structure of the samples is denser and permeated with a large number of acicular and tubular formations, indicating the presence of hydrated phases of calcium silicates and aluminates.
                    <jats:bold>Conclusion.</jats:bold>
                    These developments will reduce greenhouse gas emissions and expand the raw material base and range of cements.
                  </jats:p>

Cement-reduced ternary concrete with fly ash and silica fume for irrigation canal structures: computational mix design with single-composition experimental verification
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>Irrigation canal linings in Kazakhstan face freeze-thaw cycling, sulfate-bearing water, and abrasive sediment flow, while national programs to rehabilitate more than 14,000 km of canals create sustained demand for lower-clinker concrete. This study computationally designs a cement-reduced ternary binder (CEM I 42.5N, Ekibastuz low-calcium fly ash, and DSF-95 silica fume, 70:20:10 by mass) that replaces 30% of the cement in a plant control mixture (280 vs 400 kg/m3) while preserving total binder content, paste volume, and aggregate skeleton. The design combines particle-packing simulation, a modified Bolomey model calibrated on the measured plant control (R28 = 44.5 MPa), and Powers-model porosity. Experimentally, a laboratory composition with the same ternary binder proportions was cast and tested in 100 mm cubes, yielding a measured R28 of 52.8 MPa versus 52.6 MPa predicted (0.4% deviation); its fracture surface was examined by scanning electron microscopy. The predicted ternary mixture reaches R28 = 55.2 MPa (+24% over the control, attributable to the lower water content and the assumed packing bonus; mean-based class B40) with a 28-day capillary porosity of 0.160 versus 0.223 (−28%), lowering the paste-permeability index to about one-third of the control’s, and utilizes 120 kg of industrial by-products per cubic meter while avoiding at least 72 kg of binder-related CO2. The GOST durability grades (frost resistance, water impermeability, abrasion, sulfate resistance) are deliberately not predicted and await the ongoing laboratory campaign; the work is therefore a computational mix-design study with a single measured verification composition.</jats:p>
